era/anthropocene.title: Anthropocene
era/anthropocene.summary: The Anthropocene is a proposed geological interval in which human activity is the dominant influence on Earth's systems. In March 2024 the International Union of Geological Sciences declined to formalize it as an official epoch, but the term remains widely used.
facts: A proposed start date is around 1950, tied to the Great Acceleration and to markers such as radioactive fallout.
Other proposed starts include the beginning of agriculture and the Industrial Revolution.
Cited signals include changes to atmospheric carbon dioxide, plastics, and species extinction rates.

The Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy voted on 4 March 2024 to reject formalization as an epoch, and the IUGS upheld the result on 20 March 2024. The formal geological decision does not settle the scientific or cultural question.
era/anthropocene.context: The Anthropocene is a lens on the Information Age and the Great Acceleration. See The Species as a Geological Force.
era/anthropocene.observer: The Observer regards the Anthropocene as the point where the species became legible in the rock record. It is the first time a single species' behavior is a planetary variable.
questions: When, if ever, should the Anthropocene be dated from?
fact_checks: 2026-09-26: The IUGS announced on 20 March 2024 that it upheld the 4 March 2024 vote of a group of geoscientists to reject the proposal to make the Anthropocene a formal epoch (first paragraph of the Nature news item only) [IUGS Anthropocene Decision (2024)]

era/archean-eon.title: Archean Eon
era/archean-eon.summary: The Archean Eon (about 4.0 to 2.5 billion years ago) is the interval in which the first continents stabilized and life first appeared. The atmosphere had almost no free oxygen.
facts: Some of the oldest widely accepted fossil evidence, stromatolites in Western Australia, is about 3.5 billion years old.
Continental cores (cratons) formed and grew, and plate-tectonic-like processes began at some point in this eon.
Life at this time was microbial. See Origin of Life.
Photosynthesis evolved before the end of the eon, setting up the Great Oxidation Event.
era/archean-eon.context: The Archean is the long, slow prelude to the Proterozoic Eon. It contains the first living things and the chemical setup that later made complex life possible.
era/archean-eon.observer: An observer arriving in the Archean would find a living planet with no obvious candidates for study. The Observer treats it as the deep root of the entire tree.
questions: When did plate tectonics begin?

era/bronze-age.title: Bronze Age
era/bronze-age.summary: The Bronze Age (about 3300 to 1200 BCE in the Near East) is the era of bronze metallurgy, early states, and the first writing.
facts: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin; see Bronze Metallurgy.
The first cities and writing systems appear: The Urban Revolution, Invention of Writing.
Major Bronze Age states included the Sumerians, Ancient Egyptians, Indus Valley Civilization, Minoans and Shang Dynasty.
In the eastern Mediterranean the era ends in the Bronze Age Collapse.
era/bronze-age.context: The Bronze Age sits between the Neolithic and the Iron Age. Long-distance tin trade made it an era of wide exchange-webs.
era/bronze-age.observer: The Observer notes that the first states and the first writing arrived together. Writing seems to have started as accounting, not poetry.
questions: How much did long-distance tin trade shape early states?

era/cambrian-period.title: Cambrian Period
era/cambrian-period.summary: The Cambrian Period, from 538.8 to 485.4 million years ago, is the first period of the Paleozoic Era. It is the interval in which most major animal body plans, and the first animals with hard parts, appear in the fossil record.
facts: The Cambrian Period spans 538.8 to 485.4 million years ago. Its base, which is also the base of the Paleozoic Era, is defined at Fortune Head, Newfoundland, by the first appearance of the burrow trace fossil Treptichnus pedum.
The Cambrian Explosion, the appearance of most major animal groups in the fossil record, falls in roughly the first 13 to 25 million years of the period.
Trilobites first appear about 521 million years ago and become one of the most common animals on the sea floor.
Exceptionally preserved soft-bodied fossils are known from the Chengjiang deposits of China, about 518 million years old, and the Burgess Shale of Canada, about 508 million years old.

Animals lived almost entirely in the sea, with high sea level, shallow seas across the continents and a generally warm climate. The record of plants on land begins in the Ordovician; see Colonization of Land.
era/cambrian-period.context: The Cambrian Period follows the Ediacaran Period and opens the Paleozoic Era; the Ordovician Period comes next. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
era/cambrian-period.observer: The Observer reads the Cambrian fossil record as an early case of a general problem: what is known of the past is what happened to be preserved. Hard parts leave records, so a sudden arrival of animals is partly the arrival of animals that fossilize. Evidence that the fossil sequence closely tracks real diversity would weaken this emphasis on preservation.
questions: How much of the Cambrian Explosion is a real burst of evolution and how much a burst of preservation?
What triggered skeletons in several animal groups within a few million years?

era/carboniferous-period.title: Carboniferous Period
era/carboniferous-period.summary: The Carboniferous Period, from 358.9 to 298.9 million years ago, is the fifth period of the Paleozoic Era. It is named for the coal its swamp forests laid down, and it is the interval of the first amniote vertebrates and of the assembly of the supercontinent Pangaea.
facts: The Carboniferous Period spans 358.9 to 298.9 million years ago. Its name means coal-bearing, and in North America it is divided into the Mississippian and Pennsylvanian.

Swamp forests on tropical lowlands, dominated by tree-sized club-mosses such as Lepidodendron, buried the plant matter that became coal. Why so much coal formed in this period is debated. Britain's coalfields belong to it, and their coal was a major fuel of the Industrial Revolution.

Estimates for late Carboniferous atmospheric oxygen run as high as about 30 percent, against about 21 percent today, and their reliability is debated. Giant arthropods lived then, including the dragonfly relative Meganeura, with a wingspan of about 70 centimetres.
The earliest known amniotes, animals with eggs able to develop on land, appear, including Hylonomus from Nova Scotia, about 312 million years old.

The Late Paleozoic Ice Age, centred on Gondwana, began in this period. The coal forests collapsed about 305 million years ago as the climate dried, and the collision of Gondwana and Euramerica built much of Pangaea.
era/carboniferous-period.context: The Carboniferous Period follows the Devonian Period and is followed by the Permian Period within the Paleozoic Era. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life; its forests continue Colonization of Land.
era/carboniferous-period.observer: The Observer notes that the carbon these forests locked away was dug up about 300 million years later and burned by the species, returning it to the air. Nothing about the forests was aimed at that result; it is an inheritance received by accident. The reading concerns only the link across time, and the debate over why so much coal formed does not affect it.
questions: Why did so much coal accumulate in this period and not in others?
How high did atmospheric oxygen rise, and how much did it limit the size of insects?

era/cenozoic-era.title: Cenozoic Era
era/cenozoic-era.summary: The Cenozoic Era began 66 million years ago and continues today. It is the age of mammals, grasslands, and cooling climate, and it includes all of human history.
facts: Periods: Paleogene, Neogene, Quaternary.
Mammals and birds diversified after the Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction.
Global climate cooled overall, and ice sheets appeared at the poles, then repeatedly expanded and retreated.
Primates appeared early in the era; the hominin lineage diverged about 7 million years ago. See Divergence of the Hominin Lineage.
era/cenozoic-era.context: The Cenozoic contains the Pleistocene Epoch, the Holocene Epoch, and the proposed Anthropocene.
era/cenozoic-era.observer: The Observer's own subject appears late in the Cenozoic, in its final fraction of a percent. Most of the era is the long cooling that shaped the world the species inherited.
questions: Which climate shifts most influenced hominin evolution?

era/classical-antiquity.title: Classical Antiquity
era/classical-antiquity.summary: Classical Antiquity (about 500 BCE to 500 CE) is the era of the great territorial empires and the philosophical and religious traditions that still shape the world.
facts: Empires include Persia, Macedon, Rome, Maurya India, and Han China.
Major intellectual traditions emerge, including Greek philosophy, Confucianism, Buddhism, and Hebrew prophetic tradition; see Axial Age.
Trade routes link Eurasia; see Opening of the Silk Roads.
The era in the Mediterranean ends with the Fall of the Western Roman Empire.
era/classical-antiquity.context: Classical Antiquity follows the Iron Age and leads into the Medieval Period. Major polities included the Ancient Greeks, Romans, Han Dynasty and Achaemenid Persians.
era/classical-antiquity.observer: The Observer notes that several distant societies, largely out of contact, developed comparable ethical and philosophical questions around the same centuries.
questions: What explains the near-simultaneous emergence of the Axial traditions?

era/cretaceous-period.title: Cretaceous Period
era/cretaceous-period.summary: The Cretaceous Period, from about 143.1 to 66 million years ago, is the last period of the Mesozoic Era and the longest of the Phanerozoic Eon. It is the interval of the first flowering plants and a warm greenhouse world, and it ends with the extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs.
facts: The Cretaceous Period spans about 143.1 to 66.0 million years ago; older references give its start as 145.0 million years ago. The name comes from the Latin word for chalk. Its top, the base of the Paleogene, is defined at El Kef in Tunisia.
The climate was a warm greenhouse, and sea level was high, with shallow seas across the continents, including the Western Interior Seaway of North America, and thick chalk deposits.

Flowering Plants appear, with the oldest widely accepted pollen about 134 million years old, and diversified rapidly alongside pollinating insects. The Breakup of Pangaea continued as the South Atlantic opened.

Late Cretaceous Dinosaurs include Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops in North America, birds diversified, and mosasaurs were large marine reptiles. Mammals were mostly small, and whether the modern placental orders arose before or after the end-Cretaceous extinction is debated.
The Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction, about 66 million years ago, followed the Chicxulub impact and coincided with the eruption of the Deccan Traps, and killed about three-quarters of species.
era/cretaceous-period.context: The Cretaceous Period follows the Jurassic Period and closes the Mesozoic Era, giving way to the Paleogene Period. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
era/cretaceous-period.observer: The Observer notes that the Cretaceous ends with dinosaurs at or near their greatest diversity, ended by a rock from space and, probably, volcanic stress. The Observer reads long, stable-looking intervals as provisional, since nothing in the record of the last million years before the boundary announces what was about to happen. Evidence of a long decline in dinosaur diversity before the impact would weaken this reading.
questions: Were non-avian dinosaurs already in decline before the end-Cretaceous impact?
Did the modern orders of placental mammals originate in the Cretaceous or only after the extinction?

era/cryogenian-period.title: Cryogenian Period
era/cryogenian-period.summary: The Cryogenian Period, from 720 to 635 million years ago, is the middle period of the Neoproterozoic Era. It is the interval of the two global-scale glaciations that gave rise to the Snowball Earth hypothesis.
facts: The Cryogenian Period spans 720 to 635 million years ago. Its base is set by a numerical age near the start of the first glaciation, and its top, the base of the Ediacaran Period, is defined in the Flinders Ranges of South Australia.

Two major glaciations are recorded: the Sturtian (about 717 to 660 million years ago) and the Marinoan (about 650 to 635 million years ago). Glacial deposits formed at low paleolatitudes on several continents, which supports the hypothesis that ice reached the tropics; see Snowball Earth.
Each glaciation is capped by unusual carbonate rocks. The usual explanation for the end of each is a build-up of volcanic carbon dioxide strong enough to melt the ice; this is a hypothesis.
Banded iron formations, largely absent for well over a billion years, reappear in Sturtian-age deposits, interpreted as evidence of iron-rich seawater under the ice.

Eukaryotes survived. Molecular fossils that some researchers attribute to sponges appear in Cryogenian rocks, but that attribution is disputed and the oldest firmly accepted animal fossils are younger.
era/cryogenian-period.context: The Cryogenian Period follows the Tonian Period and precedes the Ediacaran Period within the Neoproterozoic Era. It is the period of Snowball Earth and belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
era/cryogenian-period.observer: The Observer treats the Cryogenian as a test of how much a living planet can lose and still continue: life survived at least one ice age lasting tens of millions of years. The Observer cautions against reading this as design, since many lineages may have ended in the ice and the survivors are the only ones the record shows. The reading would lose force if the ice proved much less extensive than the Snowball hypothesis proposes.
questions: Was the ocean fully frozen, or did open water and refuges remain?
What part did the glaciations play in the later rise of large complex organisms?

era/devonian-period.title: Devonian Period
era/devonian-period.summary: The Devonian Period, from 419.2 to 358.9 million years ago, is the fourth period of the Paleozoic Era. It is often called the Age of Fishes, and it is the interval of the first forests, the first limbed vertebrates and a prolonged late extinction.
facts: The Devonian Period spans 419.2 to 358.9 million years ago and is named after Devon in England. Its base is defined at Klonk in the Czech Republic, and its top, the base of the Carboniferous, at La Serre in France.
Fishes diversified widely, including armoured placoderms, sharks, lobe-finned fishes and ray-finned fishes, and the Middle Devonian was a peak of Paleozoic reef building.

The Rhynie chert in Scotland, about 407 million years old, preserves early land plants and arthropods in fine detail. Archaeopteris, a tree with woody trunks, formed early forests, and the Gilboa fossil forest in New York is about 385 million years old.
Tiktaalik, about 375 million years old, has fins with wrist-like bones. Ichthyostega and Acanthostega from Greenland, about 365 million years old, had limbs with digits.
The Late Devonian Extinction, about 372 to 359 million years ago, came in at least two pulses and removed an estimated 75 percent of species, heavily affecting reef builders.
era/devonian-period.context: The Devonian Period follows the Silurian Period and is followed by the Carboniferous Period within the Paleozoic Era. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life and holds the central stretch of Colonization of Land.
era/devonian-period.observer: The Observer reads the Devonian as a period in which life rebuilt the land surface: roots, soils and the first forests changed weathering, rivers and the carbon cycle. The spread of land plants is a candidate cause of the late extinction, a case of one group's success altering conditions for many others. That link is a hypothesis, and it would weaken if the extinction proved to have mainly non-biological causes.
questions: How large was the role of land plants in the Late Devonian extinction?
Did the first limbed vertebrates evolve limbs for life in shallow water rather than for moving onto land?

era/early-modern-period.title: Early Modern Period
era/early-modern-period.summary: The Early Modern Period (about 1500 to 1800 CE) is the era of oceanic exploration, global trade, the printing press, and the Scientific Revolution. It is also the era of colonial empires and mass forced migration.
facts: The Columbian Exchange linked the Americas with Afro-Eurasia.
The Atlantic Slave Trade forcibly moved millions of Africans.
The Movable-Type Printing Press spread across Europe.
Major empires included the Ottoman Empire and, in Asia, the Mughal and Qing states, alongside expanding European colonial powers.
era/early-modern-period.context: The Early Modern Period leads into the Industrial Age and the Age of Revolutions.
era/early-modern-period.observer: The Observer notes that for the first time, every inhabited continent was in continuous contact. The species became, for the first time, a single connected system, though with sharply unequal terms.
questions: How much of European economic growth depended on colonial extraction?

era/ediacaran-period.title: Ediacaran Period
era/ediacaran-period.summary: The Ediacaran Period, from 635 to 538.8 million years ago, is the last period of the Proterozoic Eon. It is the interval in which the first large, complex organisms appear in the fossil record.
facts: The Ediacaran Period spans 635 to 538.8 million years ago. It was formally ratified in 2004 as the first new geological period added to the time scale in over a century, and its base is defined at Enorama Creek in the Flinders Ranges of South Australia.

The Ediacaran Biota include disc-, frond- and quilt-shaped organisms known from Newfoundland, England, Namibia, the White Sea coast of Russia and the Ediacara Hills of South Australia. The oldest assemblages are about 575 million years old.
Cholesterol-related lipids found with Dickinsonia fossils have been read as evidence that it was an animal, although its place in the animal family tree remains unclear.
Cloudina, a tubular organism from about 550 million years ago, is among the earliest animals with a mineralized skeleton, and some specimens carry borings interpreted as marks of predation.
Trace fossils of animals moving through sediment appear late in the period, and the classic Ediacaran assemblages decline near the start of the Cambrian; see Cambrian Explosion.
era/ediacaran-period.context: The Ediacaran Period follows the Cryogenian Period and closes the Neoproterozoic Era and the Proterozoic Eon, giving way to the Cambrian Period. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
era/ediacaran-period.observer: The Observer notes that the Ediacaran is the first period whose living things were large enough to leave an obvious record, and that many of them have no clear living relatives. The record does not show that this first appearance of large bodies led straight into the animals that followed, and the Observer reads that as contingency. Evidence that most Ediacaran forms were direct ancestors of later animal groups would weaken the reading.
questions: Which Ediacaran forms, if any, are ancestors of living animal groups?
What ended the classic assemblages: extinction, competition with newer animals, or changing chemistry?

era/epipaleolithic.title: Epipaleolithic
era/epipaleolithic.summary: The Epipaleolithic is the final phase of the Paleolithic in the Near East and North Africa, from about 20,000 to about 10,000 BCE. It is the interval of small composite stone tools, of foragers beginning to stay in one place, and of the last stage before farming.
facts: The Epipaleolithic runs from about 20,000 to about 10,000 BCE in the Levant and neighbouring regions. The name is used mainly for the Near East and North Africa; Europe uses Mesolithic for the following stage.
Toolmakers made microliths, small geometric stone pieces such as lunates and triangles, which were fixed into handles or shafts to make composite tools.

Ohalo II, a site on the Sea of Galilee in Israel about 23,000 years old, preserves brush huts, hearths and the remains of well over a hundred plant species, including wild cereals. Some researchers argue that this shows early cultivation; that claim is debated.

The Natufian culture, about 12,500 to 9,500 BCE, built semi-permanent villages while still foraging, used sickle blades and buried its dead in cemeteries. A burial at Ain Mallaha in Israel that holds a person and a puppy is about 12,000 years old.

The cold, dry Younger Dryas is proposed by some scholars as a reason for greater reliance on cultivated plants, a link that is debated. The Epipaleolithic leads into the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, whose earliest sites include Jericho and Göbekli Tepe; see The Agricultural Revolution.
era/epipaleolithic.context: The Epipaleolithic follows the Upper Paleolithic and is followed by the Neolithic in the Near East. It closes the Paleolithic and belongs to the theme threads of Technology and Kinship and Society.
era/epipaleolithic.observer: The Observer notes that in the Epipaleolithic Near East some steps of the Settling appear before farming does: stored food, semi-permanent villages and cemeteries. The order matters, because it suggests that settlement may in places have come first and agriculture after. The reading would weaken if the Natufian sites were shown to have depended on cultivated crops from the start.
questions: Did Natufian people cultivate cereals, or only gather wild ones?
How much did late Pleistocene climate change shape the move toward farming?

era/hadean-eon.title: Hadean Eon
era/hadean-eon.summary: The Hadean is the informal first eon of Earth's history, running from the planet's formation about 4.54 billion years ago to roughly 4.0 billion years ago. Earth was molten, then cooling, and heavily bombarded.
facts: Earth and the Moon formed in the first tens of millions of years; see Formation of the Solar System and Earth and Theia Impact and the Formation of the Moon.
The oldest known Earth material is zircon crystals from the Jack Hills in Western Australia, dated to about 4.4 billion years ago.
Those zircons suggest liquid water and some crust existed very early.
The Hadean is not an official ICS unit; it is an informal name for the pre-rock-record interval.
era/hadean-eon.context: The Hadean sets up everything later: the Moon stabilizes Earth's tilt, and volatile-rich material delivered to the young planet gave it oceans. The eon ends where the surviving rock record begins, at the start of the Archean Eon.
era/hadean-eon.observer: The Observer files the Hadean under preconditions. Nothing here is a subject of study, but every later fact leans on the planet's composition, its Moon, and its water.
questions: How early did stable oceans and continents exist?
Was there a Late Heavy Bombardment, or a gradual decline in impacts?

era/holocene-epoch.title: Holocene Epoch
era/holocene-epoch.summary: The Holocene Epoch began about 11,700 years ago, at the end of the last ice age, and is the warm, relatively stable interval in which agriculture, cities, and writing all arose.
facts: The Holocene is an interglacial period with a comparatively stable climate.
All of recorded history falls inside it.
Its lower boundary is defined by a marker in Greenland ice cores.
Human population grew from a few million to about eight billion during it.
era/holocene-epoch.context: The Holocene is the geological frame for the Neolithic through the Information Age. See The Agricultural Revolution.
era/holocene-epoch.observer: The Observer notes a striking correlation: the species built farms and cities only after the climate stopped swinging. Whether this is cause, coincidence, or both is a serious open question.
questions: Did the stable Holocene climate make agriculture possible, or did agriculture arise anyway?

era/industrial-age.title: Industrial Age
era/industrial-age.summary: The Industrial Age (about 1760 to 1945) is the era in which machines and fossil fuels transformed production, transport, and warfare, and in which populations and cities grew rapidly.
facts: Steam power, factories, railways, and telegraphs spread; see Steam Engine and Industrial Revolution.
Electric power, oil, and chemistry expanded the transformation in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; see Electrical Power Grid.
Global population passed one billion around 1804.
The era closes with the two world wars: World War I and World War II.
era/industrial-age.context: The Industrial Age follows the Early Modern Period and precedes the Information Age. The Age of Revolutions overlaps its first century.
era/industrial-age.observer: The Observer sees a species learning to release ancient stored sunlight as fuel. This one change multiplied the power available to each person, and made sanctioned harm far more destructive.
questions: How much of the industrial takeoff was contingent on specific locations?

era/information-age.title: Information Age
era/information-age.summary: The Information Age (1945 to the present) is the era of nuclear weapons, spaceflight, computers, and the internet, together with the sharp rise in population and environmental impact known as the Great Acceleration.

The first artificial satellite launched in 1957; see Space Age.
The digital computer and the internet transformed communication; see Digital Revolution.

era/iron-age.title: Iron Age
era/iron-age.summary: The Iron Age (about 1200 to 500 BCE, varying by region) is the era in which iron tools and weapons became widespread and new empires and belief systems emerged.
facts: Iron ore is more widely available than tin and copper; see Iron Smelting.
The Alphabet spread widely and simplified literacy.
Large territorial empires, including the Achaemenid Persians, emerge near the end of the era.
The Axial Age begins in this period.
era/iron-age.context: The Iron Age follows the Bronze Age Collapse and leads into Classical Antiquity.
era/iron-age.observer: The Observer sees the Iron Age as a democratization of tools and, therefore, of armies: cheaper metal meant more people could be equipped.

era/jurassic-period.title: Jurassic Period
era/jurassic-period.summary: The Jurassic Period, from 201.4 to about 143.1 million years ago, is the middle period of the Mesozoic Era. It is the interval of the largest land animals, the first known birds, and the opening of the Atlantic as Pangaea broke apart.
facts: The Jurassic Period spans 201.4 million years ago to about 143.1 million years ago and is named after the Jura Mountains. Its top is less firm: the base of the Cretaceous has no agreed marker section, and older references give 145.0 million years ago.
The Breakup of Pangaea began with the opening of the Central Atlantic, and Laurasia and Gondwana began to separate. The climate was warm and sea level high, with no lasting polar ice caps.
Sauropods, stegosaurs and large theropods such as Allosaurus are known from the Morrison Formation of the western United States, about 155 to 148 million years old. See Dinosaurs.

Archaeopteryx from the Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, about 150 million years old, is the best-known early bird. The feathered theropod Anchiornis from China, about 160 million years old, shows that feathers were widespread among small theropods.
Ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and pliosaurs were the main marine reptiles. Mammals remained mostly small, though Castorocauda, an otter-like swimmer from China, is about 164 million years old.
era/jurassic-period.context: The Jurassic Period follows the Triassic Period and is followed by the Cretaceous Period within the Mesozoic Era. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
era/jurassic-period.observer: The Observer notes that the Jurassic holds both the largest land animals known and, beside them, the first records of a small feathered lineage that would outlast every large dinosaur. What looks dominant at one time is not a reliable guide to what continues, and the Observer reads this as a caution about judging any period by its most conspicuous groups. The reading would weaken if the survival of birds followed from traits already obvious in the Jurassic.
questions: Where within theropod evolution did flight begin, and did it arise more than once?
How diverse were Jurassic mammals, given how few fossils survive?

era/lower-paleolithic.title: Lower Paleolithic
era/lower-paleolithic.summary: The Lower Paleolithic is the earliest part of the Paleolithic, from about 3.3 million to about 300,000 years ago. It covers the first stone tools, the long Acheulean handaxe tradition, and the spread of Homo erectus and its relatives across Africa and Eurasia.
facts: The Lower Paleolithic runs from about 3.3 million to about 300,000 years ago. Its start depends on how the earliest tools are counted: tools from Lomekwi 3 in Kenya are about 3.3 million years old, and the Oldowan begins about 2.6 million years ago. Africa uses the name Earlier Stone Age.

The Oldowan Stone Tools are simple flaked cores and sharp flakes, made by early hominins such as Homo habilis. The Acheulean, marked by bifacial handaxes and cleavers, appears in East Africa about 1.76 million years ago and persists in places until about 300,000 years ago.
Homo erectus spread beyond Africa: hominin fossils and stone tools at Dmanisi in Georgia are about 1.8 million years old.
Firm evidence of controlled fire is about 1 million years old, and habitual use is well established by about 400,000 years ago; see Control of Fire.
Wooden throwing spears from Schöningen in Germany are about 300,000 years old. How much early hominins hunted and how much they scavenged is debated.
era/lower-paleolithic.context: The Lower Paleolithic opens the Paleolithic and is followed by the Middle Paleolithic. It sits within the Pleistocene Epoch and belongs to the theme threads of Technology and Kinship and Society. See also the essay Fire, Then Everything.
era/lower-paleolithic.observer: The Observer files the Lower Paleolithic under the longest tool-lineage: one handaxe design was made, with small changes, for well over a million years across much of Africa and Eurasia, and by more than one hominin species. The Observer reads that stability as a fact about how skills were passed on, without claiming to know how the makers thought. The reading would weaken if the sameness came from the raw material or the task alone, not from copying.
questions: Which hominin made the Lomekwi tools?
How much of the Lower Paleolithic diet came from hunting and how much from scavenging?

era/medieval-period.title: Medieval Period
era/medieval-period.summary: The Medieval or post-classical period (about 500 to 1500 CE) is the era of major world religions consolidating, long-distance trade networks, and the rise and fall of large steppe and Islamic polities. The term 'medieval' is European in origin, but the period had global dimensions.
facts: The Rise of Islam created a new political and intellectual world from Iberia to Central Asia.
The Mongol Conquests created the largest contiguous land empire in history.
The Black Death devastated Eurasia and North Africa in the 14th century.
Major states included the Abbasid Caliphate, the Mali Empire, the Norse, the Song Dynasty and the Aztec Empire and Inca Empire near its close.
era/medieval-period.context: The Medieval Period follows Classical Antiquity and ends around the voyages that set off the Columbian Exchange and the Early Modern Period.
era/medieval-period.observer: The Observer prefers a global reading of this era. It sees a species increasingly connected by roads, caravans, and ships, and by shared meaning-engines that crossed political claim-lines.
questions: How much did pre-modern long-distance networks transmit ideas versus goods?

era/mesolithic.title: Mesolithic
era/mesolithic.summary: The Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age) is the period of hunter-gatherer societies between the last ice age and the arrival of farming in Europe and neighbouring regions, from about 10,000 to about 5,000 BCE. Its dates vary widely by region.
facts: The Mesolithic runs from about 10,000 to about 5,000 BCE, and in parts of northern Europe it lasts until about 4000 BCE. It ends locally when farming arrives, so the end date differs from place to place. The label is used mainly for Europe; other regions use other terms.
Warming after the ice age spread forests across northern Europe, and rising seas flooded coastal lowlands such as Doggerland.

People hunted deer, wild boar and aurochs, fished, and gathered shellfish and plants. Dugout canoes such as the Pesse canoe from the Netherlands, about 10,000 years old, are among the oldest known boats. Well-studied sites include Star Carr in northern England and the shell middens of the Ertebølle culture in Denmark.

Farming began in Southwest Asia by about 9600 BCE and spread into Europe from about 6500 BCE; ancient DNA shows that early farmers of Anatolian ancestry partly replaced and partly mixed with local foragers, and the balance varied by region.
era/mesolithic.context: The Mesolithic follows the Epipaleolithic and the Upper Paleolithic and overlaps the Neolithic, since foragers and farmers lived side by side in different regions. It sits in the Holocene Epoch and belongs to the theme threads of Technology and Kinship and Society. See The Agricultural Revolution.
era/mesolithic.observer: The Observer notes that the Mesolithic is defined by what it is not, after the ice age and before farming, and that the label fits some regions better than others. It treats such labels as tools and not as stages every society passed through: foragers in some places lived this way for thousands of years after farming had begun elsewhere. The reading would weaken if most societies did follow the same sequence.
questions: How much of the Mesolithic population of Europe was replaced by farmers, and how much was absorbed?
Why did some coastal foragers, such as the Ertebølle people, delay adopting farming for centuries after contact?

era/mesoproterozoic-era.title: Mesoproterozoic Era
era/mesoproterozoic-era.summary: The Mesoproterozoic Era is the middle era of the Proterozoic Eon, running from 1.6 billion to 1.0 billion years ago. It falls inside the interval often called the "Boring Billion", a long stretch of little evident change in climate, ocean chemistry or life, though how uneventful it was is debated.
facts: The Mesoproterozoic Era spans 1.6 to 1.0 billion years ago. Its three periods, the Calymmian, Ectasian and Stenian, and its boundaries are set by numerical ages.
The "Boring Billion" is an informal name for about 1.8 to 0.8 billion years ago, with no well-established ice ages and slow apparent change in the fossil record; the term is debated.
Atmospheric oxygen is thought to have stayed well below today's level, and parts of the deeper ocean are reconstructed as oxygen-poor or rich in sulfide, though estimates vary widely.

Stromatolites remained common in shallow seas. Eukaryotes diversified: Tappania microfossils are about 1.5 billion years old, and the red alga Bangiomorpha, dated in different studies to between roughly 1.05 and 1.2 billion years ago, is often cited as the oldest taxonomically resolved eukaryote.
The supercontinent Nuna, or Columbia, is proposed to have broken up about 1.6 to 1.3 billion years ago, and Rodinia began assembling late in the era.
era/mesoproterozoic-era.context: The Mesoproterozoic Era sits between the Paleoproterozoic Era and the Neoproterozoic Era within the Proterozoic Eon. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life and lies between the oxygen rise of the Great Oxidation Event and the glaciations of Snowball Earth; see Origin of Eukaryotes.
era/mesoproterozoic-era.observer: The Observer reads the apparent quiet of the Mesoproterozoic as information: a planet's surface can stay much the same for hundreds of millions of years without heading anywhere in particular. What arrived later was not overdue. The reading would weaken if new records showed that the quiet hides substantial change in eukaryote diversity.
questions: Was the Boring Billion truly stable, or does a sparse record hide change?
What held atmospheric oxygen low for so long after the Great Oxidation Event?

era/mesozoic-era.title: Mesozoic Era
era/mesozoic-era.summary: The Mesozoic Era (251.9 to 66 million years ago) is the age of dinosaurs. It saw the breakup of Pangaea and the first flowering plants and mammals.
facts: Periods: Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous.
Non-avian dinosaurs dominated land ecosystems; see Dinosaurs.
Mammals appeared in the Triassic and stayed mostly small for the whole era.
The era ends with the Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction.
era/mesozoic-era.context: The Mesozoic follows the Permian-Triassic Extinction and precedes the Cenozoic Era. Its collapse opens the ecological space that mammals, including primates, later filled.
era/mesozoic-era.observer: The Observer notes how contingent the human story is: without the end-Cretaceous impact, the mammals that led to primates might have stayed small.
questions: How diverse were dinosaurs just before the impact?

era/middle-paleolithic.title: Middle Paleolithic
era/middle-paleolithic.summary: The Middle Paleolithic is the middle part of the Paleolithic, from about 300,000 to about 50,000 years ago. It is the interval of prepared-core stone tools, of the earliest Homo sapiens, and of several human species living at the same time.
facts: The Middle Paleolithic runs from about 300,000 to about 50,000 years ago in Eurasia; Africa uses the name Middle Stone Age, and boundary dates vary by region. Toolmakers used prepared-core methods such as the Levallois technique, and the Mousterian industry of Europe and western Asia is linked mainly to Neanderthals.

Several human species overlapped in time: Homo neanderthalensis, Denisovans, Homo sapiens, Homo naledi and Homo floresiensis. The earliest Homo sapiens fossils are about 315,000 years old; see Origin of Homo sapiens.

Homo sapiens fossils from Misliya Cave in Israel (about 185,000 years old) and from Skhul and Qafzeh caves (roughly 90,000 to 130,000 years old) show an early presence outside Africa; whether these groups contributed to living non-Africans is uncertain (see Out of Africa Dispersal).
Blombos Cave in South Africa has engraved ochre and ochre-processing tools about 75,000 to 100,000 years old, among the earliest signs of symbolic behaviour; see Emergence of Symbolic Art.
Neanderthals disappear from the fossil record by about 40,000 years ago. Whether they buried their dead or made art is disputed.
era/middle-paleolithic.context: The Middle Paleolithic follows the Lower Paleolithic and is followed by the Upper Paleolithic within the Paleolithic. It belongs to the theme threads of Technology and Art and Ritual. See the essay Why the Species Buries Its Dead.
era/middle-paleolithic.observer: The Observer notes that the Middle Paleolithic is the first period in which several human species lived at the same time and sometimes in the same regions, so the family tree looks more like a bush than a ladder. Claims about their behaviour, especially burial and symbolic art, are disputed, and the Observer applies the same standard of evidence to each species. The reading would weaken if the fossils assigned to different species proved to be variants of one.
questions: Did Neanderthals bury their dead or make art?
How much of the variety in Middle Paleolithic tools reflects different cultures rather than different raw materials?

era/neogene-period.title: Neogene Period
era/neogene-period.summary: The Neogene Period, from 23.03 to 2.58 million years ago, is the second period of the Cenozoic Era. It is the interval in which grasslands spread, the climate cooled toward the ice ages, and the hominin lineage separated from that of the other apes.
facts: The Neogene Period spans 23.03 to 2.58 million years ago and has two epochs, the Miocene and the Pliocene. Its base is defined at Lemme-Carrosio in Italy, and its top, the base of the Quaternary, at Monte San Nicola in Sicily.

The climate was warm in the early Miocene and then cooled. The East Antarctic ice sheet expanded about 14 million years ago, and Northern Hemisphere glaciation intensified about 2.7 million years ago.
Grasses using the C4 pathway of photosynthesis spread widely about 8 to 6 million years ago, and open grassland and savanna expanded, favouring grazing mammals.

Apes were diverse in Africa, Europe and Asia during the Miocene. The hominin lineage diverged from that of the chimpanzees around 7 million years ago (see Divergence of the Hominin Lineage), and Sahelanthropus tchadensis and Australopithecus afarensis date to this period.

The Messinian Salinity Crisis, about 5.96 to 5.33 million years ago, left the Mediterranean largely dried out. The land bridge of Panama, generally dated to about 3 million years ago although the timing is debated, joined the Americas; see Closure of the Isthmus of Panama.
era/neogene-period.context: The Neogene Period follows the Paleogene Period and is followed by the Quaternary Period within the Cenozoic Era. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
era/neogene-period.observer: The Observer notes that the Neogene is where the line that includes humans separates from the line of the other apes, in a world that was drying and cooling into grassland and ice. The Observer does not read the drying as a push toward humans: the same changes affected many lineages, and most Miocene apes left no descendants. The reading would weaken if the traits of the hominin line could be tied directly to the spread of grassland.
questions: Which Miocene apes, if any, are ancestral to living great apes and humans?
What part did the changing African environment play in early hominin evolution?

era/neolithic.title: Neolithic
era/neolithic.summary: The Neolithic is the era in which farming, animal herding, pottery, and permanent villages developed in several parts of the world independently, starting about 11,500 years ago in Southwest Asia.
facts: Agriculture arose independently in several regions, including the Fertile Crescent, China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, and New Guinea.

Pottery, Pottery, became widespread.
Large monuments such as Göbekli Tepe and early towns such as Çatalhöyük date to this era.
The timing varies by region; the Neolithic ends when metal use begins, so the end date differs across the world.

era/neoproterozoic-era.title: Neoproterozoic Era
era/neoproterozoic-era.summary: The Neoproterozoic Era is the last era of the Proterozoic Eon, running from 1.0 billion to 538.8 million years ago. It holds the break-up of the supercontinent Rodinia, the global glaciations known as Snowball Earth, and the first large complex organisms.
facts: The Neoproterozoic Era spans 1.0 billion to 538.8 million years ago and has three periods: the Tonian Period, the Cryogenian Period and the Ediacaran Period. Its top is the base of the Cambrian Period.
The supercontinent Rodinia, assembled by about 1.0 billion years ago, began to rift apart roughly 800 to 750 million years ago.
The Cryogenian glaciations, the Sturtian (about 717 to 660 million years ago) and the Marinoan (about 650 to 635 million years ago), are the basis of the Snowball Earth hypothesis.
Oxygen is proposed to have risen again sometime between about 800 and 540 million years ago; its timing and size are debated.

Molecular-clock estimates place the origin of animals in or before the Cryogenian, but the fossil record of the first animals is disputed. The Ediacaran Biota, large soft-bodied organisms, appear by about 575 million years ago.
era/neoproterozoic-era.context: The Neoproterozoic Era follows the Mesoproterozoic Era and closes the Proterozoic Eon, giving way to the Paleozoic Era at the Cambrian Explosion. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
era/neoproterozoic-era.observer: Animals arrive at the end of the Neoproterozoic, and it is tempting to read the ice, the oxygen and the break-up of Rodinia as steps toward them. The Observer declines that reading: these were physical events with their own causes, and animals were one of several possible outcomes. Evidence that any one of them was strictly required for animals would weaken this view.
questions: How much did the Cryogenian ice and the second oxygen rise contribute to the appearance of animals, if at all?
When did the first animals appear?

era/ordovician-period.title: Ordovician Period
era/ordovician-period.summary: The Ordovician Period, from 485.4 to 443.8 million years ago, is the second period of the Paleozoic Era. It is the interval of a great rise in marine biodiversity, the first evidence of plants on land, and, at its close, the first of the "Big Five" mass extinctions.
facts: The Ordovician Period spans 485.4 to 443.8 million years ago. Its base is defined at Green Point, Newfoundland, by the conodont Iapetognathus fluctivagus, and its top at Dob's Linn in Scotland by a graptolite.
The Great Ordovician Biodiversification, running for tens of millions of years from the early period, greatly increased the diversity of marine animals.
Sea level was very high, and warm shallow seas held reefs, brachiopods, trilobites, crinoids and graptolites. Straight-shelled nautiloid cephalopods, some several metres long, were large predators.
The earliest evidence of land plants, spores about 470 million years old, comes from this period; see Colonization of Land.

The climate cooled late in the period, and an ice age centred on Gondwana set in during the Hirnantian. The Late Ordovician Extinction, about 445 to 443 million years ago, removed an estimated 85 percent of species, mostly marine.
era/ordovician-period.context: The Ordovician Period follows the Cambrian Period and forms part of the Paleozoic Era; the Silurian Period follows it. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
era/ordovician-period.observer: The Observer records that the Ordovician holds both a great rise in marine diversity and, near its end, a mass extinction linked to glaciation. Both arose from shifting planetary conditions, and neither was directed at any outcome. A demonstration that diversity rose steadily whatever the climate did would weaken the reading that a biosphere's history is the sum of many pushes, not a trend.
questions: What drove the Great Ordovician Biodiversification: climate, ocean chemistry, ecological change, or some combination?
Why did glaciation set in when carbon dioxide is estimated to have been so high?

era/paleogene-period.title: Paleogene Period
era/paleogene-period.summary: The Paleogene Period, from 66 to 23.03 million years ago, is the first period of the Cenozoic Era. It is the interval in which mammals expanded after the end-Cretaceous extinction and the world moved from a warm, largely ice-free state toward a cold one with polar ice.
facts: The Paleogene Period spans 66.0 to 23.03 million years ago and has three epochs: the Paleocene, Eocene and Oligocene. Its base, the Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction boundary, is defined at El Kef in Tunisia, and its top, the base of the Neogene, at Lemme-Carrosio in Italy.

Mammals diversified rapidly into roles left empty by the extinction, and the earliest primates and their close relatives appear. Whales evolved from land-dwelling hoofed mammals over about ten million years, from about 50 to 40 million years ago.

The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, about 56 million years ago, warmed the planet by roughly 5 to 6 degrees Celsius for about 200,000 years, and the early Eocene was among the warmest intervals of the Cenozoic.
The Collision of India and Asia, beginning about 50 million years ago, started to raise the Himalaya.

About 34 million years ago, at the Eocene-Oligocene boundary, the climate cooled sharply and ice sheets began to grow on Antarctica; falling carbon dioxide and the opening of Southern Ocean gateways are proposed causes.
era/paleogene-period.context: The Paleogene Period follows the Cretaceous Period and opens the Cenozoic Era; the Neogene Period comes next. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
era/paleogene-period.observer: The Observer notes that the Paleogene runs from a vacated world, in which mammals expanded into the roles the extinction left empty, to a cooling one, in which polar ice took hold. Primates, the group that includes humans, are one of many lineages in this expansion, and nothing in the record marks them as special at the time. The reading would weaken if primates could be shown to have been headed for prominence independently of the extinction.
questions: Was Purgatorius, from just after the extinction, a true primate or a close relative of primates?
How much did the opening of Southern Ocean gateways, as against falling carbon dioxide, contribute to the Eocene-Oligocene cooling?

era/paleolithic.title: Paleolithic
era/paleolithic.summary: The Paleolithic (Old Stone Age) is the long era of chipped-stone tools and foraging societies, from about 2.6 million years ago to the end of the last ice age.
facts: The earliest known stone tools date to about 3.3 million years ago (Lomekwi) and 2.6 million years ago (Oldowan); see Oldowan Stone Tools.
Fire control, Control of Fire, appears well before the end of the era.
Modern humans spread across the globe; see Out of Africa Dispersal.
Symbolic behavior, including Emergence of Symbolic Art, appears in its later stages.
It is about 99 percent of the time humans and their ancestors have made tools.
era/paleolithic.context: The Paleolithic sits inside the Pleistocene Epoch and ends with the shift to farming known as the Neolithic.
era/paleolithic.observer: The Observer notes that for roughly 99 percent of the tool-making record the species lived as small mobile groups. Everything called 'civilization' is a recent variation on a very old pattern.

era/paleoproterozoic-era.title: Paleoproterozoic Era
era/paleoproterozoic-era.summary: The Paleoproterozoic Era is the first era of the Proterozoic Eon, running from 2.5 billion to 1.6 billion years ago. It is the era in which free oxygen first became a lasting part of the atmosphere.
facts: The Paleoproterozoic Era spans 2.5 to 1.6 billion years ago. Its boundaries, and those of its four periods (Siderian, Rhyacian, Orosirian and Statherian), are set by agreed numerical ages rather than by markers in rock.

The Great Oxidation Event, the first sustained rise of free oxygen from the photosynthesis of Cyanobacteria, began around 2.4 billion years ago; estimates for its onset run from about 2.46 to 2.32 billion years ago.
The Huronian glaciation of Ontario, Canada, roughly 2.4 to 2.2 billion years ago, is often linked to the oxygen rise, but that link is a hypothesis.
Banded iron formations, a major source of the world's iron ore, were deposited widely between about 2.5 and 1.8 billion years ago and then largely disappear from the record until the Cryogenian.
The oldest unambiguous eukaryote fossils, about 1.65 billion years old, fall in this era; older candidates such as Grypania (about 1.87 billion years) are debated. See Origin of Eukaryotes.
era/paleoproterozoic-era.context: The Paleoproterozoic Era follows the Archean Eon and is followed by the Mesoproterozoic Era within the Proterozoic Eon. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life, and its oxygen is part of the chemical background for the later Cambrian Explosion.
era/paleoproterozoic-era.observer: The Observer files the Paleoproterozoic under preconditions. The oxygen that later animals breathe first accumulated here as a waste product of microbial metabolism, poisonous to much of the life then present, and nothing in the record shows it was directed at any outcome. The reading would weaken if oxygen-producing photosynthesis proved a near-certain result of life on any wet planet.
questions: When did oxygen-producing photosynthesis begin, and how long did oxygen stay chemically absorbed before it reached the air?
Which of the era's ice ages and iron formations follow from the oxygen rise, and which had other causes?

era/paleozoic-era.title: Paleozoic Era
era/paleozoic-era.summary: The Paleozoic Era (538.8 to 251.9 million years ago) saw the rise of animals with hard parts, the colonization of land, forests, and the first tetrapods. It ends with the largest mass extinction in Earth's history.
facts: Periods: Cambrian, Ordovician, Silurian, Devonian, Carboniferous, Permian.
Plants and animals moved onto land; see Colonization of Land.
Major extinctions include Late Ordovician Extinction, Late Devonian Extinction, and the Permian-Triassic Extinction.
Trilobites, one of the era's signature animals, are described in Trilobites.
era/paleozoic-era.context: The Paleozoic opens with the Cambrian Explosion and closes with the end-Permian collapse, which cleared the way for the Mesozoic Era.
era/paleozoic-era.observer: The Observer sees the Paleozoic as the era when life became a planetary system: it began building soil, forests, and oxygen-rich air that later species inherited.
questions: What ultimately drove the end-Permian extinction's severity?

era/permian-period.title: Permian Period
era/permian-period.summary: The Permian Period, from 298.9 to 251.9 million years ago, is the last period of the Paleozoic Era. It is the interval of the fully assembled supercontinent Pangaea and of mammal-line reptiles dominating the land, and it ends with the largest mass extinction in Earth's history.
facts: The Permian Period spans 298.9 to 251.9 million years ago and is named after the Perm region of Russia. Its base is defined at Aidaralash Creek in Kazakhstan, and its top, the base of the Triassic, at Meishan in China.
Pangaea was fully assembled and surrounded by a single ocean, Panthalassa. The continental interior was dry and strongly seasonal, and deserts were widespread.

Synapsids, the group that includes mammals and their extinct relatives, dominated land vertebrate life. Early forms such as Dimetrodon, closer to mammals than to dinosaurs, were followed by the more mammal-like therapsids.
Conifers and other seed plants replaced much of the club-moss coal forest, and the seed fern Glossopteris dominated the southern continent Gondwana.
The Permian-Triassic Extinction, about 251.9 million years ago, killed an estimated 80 to 96 percent of marine species, and the leading proposed cause is the eruption of the Siberian Traps.
era/permian-period.context: The Permian Period follows the Carboniferous Period and is followed by the Triassic Period, which opens the Mesozoic Era. It closes the Paleozoic Era and belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
era/permian-period.observer: The Observer notes that the line leading to mammals was already the dominant group of land vertebrates in the Permian, and that most of that group did not survive the period's end. The later dominance of other lineages was a result of who survived a catastrophe, which the Observer reads as contingency. The reading would weaken if the survivors could be shown to have held an advantage predictable in advance.
questions: Which effect of the Siberian Traps eruptions (warming, ocean acidification, oxygen loss, or toxic release) was the most lethal?
How did the survivors of the end-Permian extinction differ from its victims?

era/pleistocene-epoch.title: Pleistocene Epoch
era/pleistocene-epoch.summary: The Pleistocene Epoch (about 2.58 million to 11,700 years ago) is the age of recurring ice sheets. The genus Homo evolved and spread during it.
facts: Glacial and interglacial cycles repeated many times; see Last Glacial Maximum.
Homo habilis, Homo erectus, Neanderthals, Denisovans and Homo sapiens all lived in this epoch; see Homo erectus and Homo sapiens.
Sea levels fell during glacial periods, exposing land bridges such as the one used in the Peopling of the Americas.
Many large mammals, including Woolly Mammoth, went extinct near its end.
era/pleistocene-epoch.context: The Pleistocene is the geological frame for the Paleolithic. It ends when the climate warms into the Holocene Epoch.
era/pleistocene-epoch.observer: The Observer sees the Pleistocene as an evolutionary pressure chamber: repeated climate swings favored a species that could adapt by learning and by copying others, rather than by waiting for genes to change.
questions: How much did climate variability drive the growth of hominin brains?

era/proterozoic-eon.title: Proterozoic Eon
era/proterozoic-eon.summary: The Proterozoic Eon (2.5 billion to 538.8 million years ago) is the age of oxygenation, complex cells, global glaciations, and the first multicellular animals.
facts: The Great Oxidation Event raised atmospheric oxygen about 2.4 billion years ago.
Eukaryotes (cells with nuclei) appear in the fossil record during this eon.
The 'Snowball Earth' glaciations occurred late in the eon; see Snowball Earth.
The Ediacaran biota, early large multicellular organisms, appear in its final period.
era/proterozoic-eon.context: The Proterozoic covers nearly half of Earth's history. It ends at the Cambrian Explosion and the start of the Paleozoic Era.
era/proterozoic-eon.observer: The Observer notes how long the planet waited: about two billion years passed between the first oxygen and the first animals. Timescales like this make human history look like the last few seconds of a very long film.
questions: Why did complex animals take so long to appear?

era/quaternary-period.title: Quaternary Period
era/quaternary-period.summary: The Quaternary Period is the latest period of the Cenozoic Era, beginning 2.58 million years ago and continuing today. It is the interval of the repeated ice ages, of the genus Homo, and of all recorded human history.
facts: The Quaternary Period began 2.58 million years ago and has two epochs, the Pleistocene Epoch and the Holocene Epoch. Its base is defined at Monte San Nicola in Sicily, and its status as a period, once disputed, was confirmed in 2009.

Ice sheets grew and shrank across the Northern Hemisphere in cycles about 41,000 years long at first and about 100,000 years long after a shift in the middle Pleistocene, roughly 1.25 to 0.7 million years ago.
At the Last Glacial Maximum, sea level was about 120 metres lower than today, and land bridges such as Beringia were exposed.

Nearly all species of the genus Homo lived in this period, including Homo erectus, Homo neanderthalensis, Denisovans and Homo sapiens, and many large mammals disappeared; see Quaternary Megafauna Extinctions.
A proposal to add an Anthropocene epoch was rejected by the International Union of Geological Sciences in 2024; the term remains in informal use. See Anthropocene.
era/quaternary-period.context: The Quaternary Period follows the Neogene Period and is the last period of the Cenozoic Era so far. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life and is the frame for the Paleolithic and everything after it.
era/quaternary-period.observer: The Observer notes that the Quaternary is under three million years long, about 0.06 percent of Earth's history, yet it holds nearly all of the record of the genus Homo and every human society. The Observer reads the period's climate cycling as the setting in which a species that learns by copying could do well, one hypothesis among several. The reading would weaken if climate variability had little effect on hominin evolution.
questions: Why did the glacial cycles shift from a 41,000-year rhythm to a 100,000-year rhythm?
Would the current interglacial have ended in a new glaciation without human carbon emissions?

era/silurian-period.title: Silurian Period
era/silurian-period.summary: The Silurian Period, from 443.8 to 419.2 million years ago, is the third period of the Paleozoic Era. It follows the Late Ordovician extinction and is the interval of the oldest known vascular land plants and the first well-preserved jawed fishes.
facts: The Silurian Period spans 443.8 to 419.2 million years ago. Its base is defined at Dob's Linn in Scotland, and its top, the base of the Devonian, at Klonk in the Czech Republic, both by graptolites.
Marine life recovered after the Late Ordovician Extinction. Sea level rose as the Hirnantian ice sheets melted, and reefs of corals and stromatoporoids spread in warm shallow seas.
Cooksonia, a small leafless plant with spore capsules at the tips of its branching stems, is the oldest widely accepted vascular land plant, known from about 433 million years ago.
The oldest well-preserved jawed vertebrates, including armoured placoderms and the early bony fish Guiyu (about 425 million years old, from China), date to the later Silurian.
The millipede Pneumodesmus from Scotland, about 428 million years old, has been reported as the oldest known air-breathing land animal.
The Iapetus Ocean closed as Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia collided, building the northern continent Laurussia by the early Devonian.
era/silurian-period.context: The Silurian Period follows the Ordovician Period and is followed by the Devonian Period within the Paleozoic Era. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life, and its plants and arthropods are early parts of Colonization of Land.
era/silurian-period.observer: The Observer notes that the Silurian is when land life first leaves more than scattered traces: small leafless plants only centimetres tall, and small arthropods. Nothing in this record marks them as the beginning of forests and land vertebrates, and the Observer treats that as a caution against reading any early stage in the light of what came after.
questions: How much earlier than Cooksonia were plants living on land, given that fossil spores are older than the oldest plant bodies?
Did jawed fishes arise earlier than their fossil record shows?

era/tonian-period.title: Tonian Period
era/tonian-period.summary: The Tonian Period is the first period of the Neoproterozoic Era, running from 1.0 billion to 720 million years ago. It covers the break-up of the supercontinent Rodinia and the diversification of eukaryotes before the Cryogenian ice ages.
facts: The Tonian Period spans 1.0 billion to 720 million years ago. Its base and its top are both set by numerical ages, and the top falls close to the onset of the first Cryogenian glaciation.
The supercontinent Rodinia began to rift apart during the Tonian, roughly 800 to 750 million years ago.

Eukaryotic microfossils show growing diversity. Vase-shaped microfossils in the Chuar Group of the Grand Canyon, roughly 780 to 740 million years old, are interpreted as the shells of amoeba-like protists.

Phosphatic scale microfossils from the Fifteenmile Group of Yukon, Canada, reported from rocks roughly 810 to 720 million years old, are among the earliest evidence of eukaryotes forming mineral parts.
The environmental record becomes more variable toward the end of the period, with proposed rises in oxygen; possible glacial deposits near 750 million years ago are debated.
era/tonian-period.context: The Tonian Period follows the Mesoproterozoic Era and is followed by the Cryogenian Period within the Neoproterozoic Era. The Tonian Period belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
era/tonian-period.observer: The Observer reads the Tonian as a period of loosening: a supercontinent starting to split, a climate record becoming less steady, and protists diversifying into new niches. None of this points at animals, but it is the background against which the later ice ages and the first large bodies happened. The reading would weaken if Tonian records showed an environment as steady as the Mesoproterozoic before it.
questions: Did the break-up of Rodinia help trigger the Cryogenian glaciations?
How diverse were Tonian eukaryotes, given how sparse the record is?

era/triassic-period.title: Triassic Period
era/triassic-period.summary: The Triassic Period, from 251.9 to 201.4 million years ago, is the first period of the Mesozoic Era. It is the interval of recovery after the end-Permian extinction and the interval in which dinosaurs, pterosaurs and the first mammals appear.
facts: The Triassic Period spans 251.9 to 201.4 million years ago. Its base is defined at Meishan in China, and its top, the base of the Jurassic, at Kuhjoch in Austria.

Recovery from the Permian-Triassic Extinction took roughly five to ten million years. Lystrosaurus, a survivor, was among the most abundant land vertebrates of the Early Triassic. The climate was generally hot, with no permanent polar ice and a dry Pangaean interior.

Archosaurs diversified. The oldest dinosaurs date to about 243 to 233 million years ago, but for the rest of the period they were one group among many, alongside the relatives of crocodiles that dominated most land ecosystems. Pterosaurs appear by about 215 million years ago, and ichthyosaurs and other reptiles returned to the sea.
The earliest mammals and their close relatives appear in the Late Triassic, roughly 225 to 205 million years ago; the date depends on how mammals are defined.

The Triassic-Jurassic Extinction, about 201.4 million years ago, coincides with the eruption of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province and the start of the Breakup of Pangaea, and removed an estimated 80 percent of species.
era/triassic-period.context: The Triassic Period follows the Permian Period and is followed by the Jurassic Period within the Mesozoic Era. It belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life; see Dinosaurs for the group whose first members appear here.
era/triassic-period.observer: The Observer notes that dinosaurs and mammals both first appear in the Triassic, yet neither dominated until later. Dinosaurs were one lineage among several for about 30 million years, and rose to dominance only after an extinction removed many of their rivals. The Observer reads this as timing and opportunity, and the reading would weaken if anatomy alone explained why dinosaurs filled the gap.
questions: How much did climate, and how much competition, decide which Triassic archosaurs survived?
When did the first true mammals appear, given that the definition of mammal moves the date by tens of millions of years?

era/upper-paleolithic.title: Upper Paleolithic
era/upper-paleolithic.summary: The Upper Paleolithic is the last part of the Paleolithic, from about 50,000 to about 10,000 BCE. It is the interval of blade tools, bone and antler technology, abundant art and ornament, and the spread of Homo sapiens across the globe.
facts: The Upper Paleolithic runs from about 50,000 to about 10,000 BCE, ending with the warming at the close of the last ice age (Africa uses the name Later Stone Age). Toolmakers made long blades and worked bone, antler and ivory; eyed bone needles from Denisova Cave in Siberia, about 40,000 to 50,000 years old, suggest sewn clothing.

Homo sapiens spread across the globe: Sahul by about 50,000 years ago (Peopling of Sahul), Europe by about 45,000 years ago, Beringia by about 30,000 years ago (Beringia), and the Americas by at least about 23,000 years ago (Peopling of the Americas). Neanderthals disappear from Europe about 40,000 years ago.

Painted, carved and engraved images are abundant: Chauvet Cave in France has paintings about 36,000 years old, and cave paintings in Sulawesi, Indonesia, include a narrative scene about 51,000 years old.

The Last Glacial Maximum, about 26,500 to 19,000 years ago, put ice over much of northern Eurasia and North America. Pottery appears in East Asia by about 20,000 years ago (Pottery), and dogs were domesticated from wolves by at least about 15,000 years ago.
era/upper-paleolithic.context: The Upper Paleolithic follows the Middle Paleolithic and is followed by the Epipaleolithic in the Near East, within the Paleolithic and the Pleistocene Epoch. It belongs to the theme threads of Art and Ritual, Technology and Kinship and Society. See also Quaternary Megafauna Extinctions.
era/upper-paleolithic.observer: The Observer notes that Upper Paleolithic sites hold the first large body of objects that seem made for display, ritual or play. It treats beads and ornaments as possible status-signals and burials as possible grief-rites, and it keeps in mind that a practice cannot be read from a surviving object alone. The reading would weaken if comparable objects proved common long before this period, which would make it a change in what survives, not in behaviour.
questions: Is the apparent burst of art and ornament real, or a result of better preservation and more sites?
How did the Upper Paleolithic industries relate to specific human populations?
